Build one network, or one network per time window, from bipartite links

Source: R/build_dynamic_networks.R
build_dynamic_networks.Rd

The first step of the networkflow pipeline. Research data rarely come as a network: they come as a table of links between two kinds of entities, such as articles and the references they cite, authors and the papers they sign, or accounts and the hashtags they use. build_dynamic_networks() projects this two-mode (bipartite) relation onto the first kind of entity: two source_id entities (e.g. two articles) are linked when they share target_id entities (e.g. references). With time_variable and time_window, it builds one such network per time window, which is the starting point of a dynamic analysis.

Write \(a_{ij} = 1\) when source \(i\) is linked to target \(j\). The raw strength of the tie between sources \(i\) and \(k\) is the number of targets they share, $$c_{ik} = \sum_j a_{ij} a_{kj} = |R_i \cap R_k|,$$ with \(R_i\) the set of targets of \(i\). When sources are citing documents and targets their references, this is bibliographic coupling (Kessler 1963) . Swapping the roles (cited documents as source_id, citing documents as target_id) gives a co-citation network (Small 1973) .

Raw counts favour sources with many targets (articles with long bibliographies), and most pairs share a target or two by chance. The two projection_methods answer this problem in different ways:

  • "structured" normalises the counts with a bibliometric similarity measure computed by biblionetwork and keeps the pairs sharing at least edges_threshold targets;

  • "statistical" keeps only the ties that are stronger than expected under a null model of random co-occurrence, using the backbone package (Neal 2014, 2022) .

Usage

build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes,
  directed_edges,
  source_id,
  target_id,
  document_id = NULL,
  projection_on = c("source", "target"),
  projection_method = c("structured", "statistical"),
  cooccurrence_method = c("coupling_angle", "coupling_strength", "coupling_similarity"),
  edges_threshold = 1,
  model = c("sdsm", "fdsm", "fixedfill", "fixedrow", "fixedcol"),
  alpha = NULL,
  backbone_args = list(),
  time_variable = NULL,
  time_in = c("nodes", "edges"),
  time_unit = NULL,
  time_window = NULL,
  window_step = NULL,
  compute_size = FALSE,
  keep_singleton = FALSE,
  filter_components = FALSE,
  ...,
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

nodes

A data frame with one row per source entity (e.g. one row per article) and its metadata (authors, year, title...). Not modified.

directed_edges

A data frame of bipartite links, one row per source_id -> target_id link (e.g. article -> cited reference). Duplicated links are counted once. Not modified.

source_id

Character scalar, the column identifying the entities that become the nodes of the network. It must exist in both nodes and directed_edges, with one row per value in nodes.

target_id

Character scalar, the column of directed_edges with the entities that create the links (e.g. references).

document_id

Optional column of directed_edges identifying the document through which each link exists. With it, source_id entities are not documents but entities that publish documents (authors, journals, institutions) and a reference cited by several documents of an entity counts several times, following biblionetwork::coupling_entity(). Only for projection_method = "structured" with "coupling_angle" or "coupling_strength".

projection_on

"source" (default) links the source_id entities that share target_id entities (bibliographic coupling: articles sharing references). "target" links the target_id entities that share source_id entities (co-citation: cited documents linked when they are cited by the same documents). With "target", nodes is keyed by target_id.

projection_method

"structured" (default) or "statistical", see the description and the details.

cooccurrence_method

For projection_method = "structured", the similarity measure used as edge weight: "coupling_angle", "coupling_strength" or "coupling_similarity" (see the details). There is no default: the choice must be explicit.

edges_threshold

For projection_method = "structured", the minimum number of shared targets for two sources to be linked (1 by default).

model

For projection_method = "statistical", the null model of backbone::backbone_from_projection(): "sdsm", "fdsm", "fixedfill", "fixedrow" or "fixedcol".

alpha

For projection_method = "statistical", the significance level of the test of each tie. Lower values keep fewer edges.

backbone_args

Optional list of further arguments for backbone::backbone_from_projection() (e.g. mtc = "holm" to correct for multiple tests). alpha or model given here override the arguments of the function.

time_variable

Optional name of a column with the time of each node (or of each link, with time_in = "edges"): a number (e.g. a year), a Date, a POSIXct, or an ISO date written as text ("2001-03", "2001-03-15"). Years written as text ("2001") are numbers. Without it, a single network is built.

time_in

"nodes" (default): time_variable is a column of nodes and a window selects the nodes of the period. "edges": time_variable is a column of directed_edges (e.g. the year of the citing document) and a window selects the links of the period, the nodes being those with a link in the window. Use "edges" for co-citation, whose period is the one of the citing documents, and for entities without a date of their own (authors).

time_unit

For dates only: the unit in which windows are counted, "year" (default), "quarter", "month", "week" (starting on Mondays) or "day". For numbers, the unit is the one of the variable and time_unit must stay NULL.

time_window

Optional whole number, the width of each window in time_units (or in units of the variable): 10 for ten years, 12 with time_unit = "month" for a year. NULL builds a single network.

window_step

Optional whole number, the number of units between the starts of two windows. NULL (default) gives successive windows (window_step = time_window); 1 slides the window one unit at a time (1975-1984, 1976-1985...); 3 with time_unit = "month" and a window of 12 gives a yearly window every quarter.

compute_size

Logical. If TRUE, adds a node_size column: the number of times each node is a target of the sources of the same window (for a coupling network, the number of citations received within the corpus). It requires nodes to contain the target_id column.

keep_singleton

Logical. If FALSE (default), nodes without any edge are removed.

filter_components

Logical. If TRUE, keeps only the main component(s) with filter_components().

...

Arguments passed to filter_components() (e.g. nb_components).

verbose

Logical. If TRUE (default), reports the steps.

Value

A tbl_graph (undirected) if time_variable is NULL; otherwise a list of tbl_graphs named after their window (e.g. "1975-1984"), in chronological order, whose nodes have a time_window column. Edges have a weight column for the structured method.

Details

Similarity measures (projection_method = "structured"). With \(L_i = |R_i|\) the number of targets of source \(i\), \(N\) the number of sources and \(f_j\) the number of sources linked to target \(j\), the three measures computed by biblionetwork are:

  • "coupling_angle", the cosine of Sen and Gan (1983) : $$w_{ik} = \frac{|R_i \cap R_k|}{\sqrt{L_i L_k}};$$

  • "coupling_strength" (Vladutz and Cook 1984; Shen et al. 2019) , where a shared target counts less when it is linked to many sources, in the spirit of an inverse document frequency: $$w_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \log(N / f_j)}{L_i L_k};$$

  • "coupling_similarity", the idf-weighted cosine of Shen et al. (2019) : each source is described by a vector with one component per target, equal to \(\sqrt{\log(N / f_j)}\), and the weight is the cosine of the vectors of two sources, with \(S_i = \sum_{j \in R_i} \log(N / f_j)\) the weighted size of the bibliography: $$w_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \log(N / f_j)}{\sqrt{S_i S_k}}.$$ Like the coupling angle, it lies between 0 and 1; like the coupling strength, it discounts the targets linked to many sources. (Versions 0.1.1 and earlier of biblionetwork computed this measure wrongly: use biblionetwork 0.1.1.9000 or later.)

Targets linked to a single source cannot create a tie and are dropped before the computation. The threshold applies to the raw count \(|R_i \cap R_k|\), not to the weight: edges_threshold = 2 keeps the pairs of articles that share at least two references, a common choice to remove ties that one shared classic is enough to create. The measures differ in how they treat very cited targets and long target lists; in practice, clusters are often robust to the choice, but it is worth checking on one's own data.

Statistical backbones (projection_method = "statistical"). Instead of fixing a threshold, the backbone approach asks, for each pair, whether the observed number of shared targets is larger than in random bipartite networks that preserve some properties of the observed one: the degrees of sources and targets on average ("sdsm", the stochastic degree sequence model) or exactly ("fdsm"), or only the total number of links ("fixedfill") (Neal 2014; Domagalski et al. 2021) . Edges are kept when the test is significant at level alpha; the resulting network is unweighted. This is slower, but each edge can be read as a tie unlikely to be due to chance.

Time windows. Time is counted in whole units: the values of a numeric variable, or years, quarters, months, weeks or days for dates. A window starting at unit \(s\) and \(w\) units wide (time_window) gathers the nodes (or links) with \(s \le t < s + w\), and the network is computed as if the corpus were limited to them. A new window starts every window_step units: successive windows (the default) give independent snapshots, a step of 1 slides the window and smooths the evolution of the networks, at the price of many networks sharing most of their nodes. The last window may be shorter than the others when the period is not a multiple of the step (a warning is given); windows are labelled by their first and last unit ("1975-1984", "2001-01 to 2001-12"). The choice of the window is substantive: long enough for each network to have enough nodes (a few dozen at least) to show a structure, and short enough for changes to be visible. For documents that follow each other quickly (central bank statements, news, posts), months or weeks make sense, with a window wide enough to contain enough documents.

Beyond bibliographic coupling. Nothing in the function is specific to citations. The two sides of the links can be any two kinds of entities:

  • Co-citation (Small 1973) : with projection_on = "target", cited documents are linked when the same documents cite them. Windows should follow the citing documents: put their year in directed_edges and use time_in = "edges".

  • Author (or journal, institution) coupling (Zhao and Strotmann 2008) : with document_id, authors are linked when the documents they sign cite the same references.

  • Co-authorship and other co-occurrences: authors and the documents they sign, accounts and the hashtags they use, members and the boards they sit on: any two-mode table.

Identifiers of references. Every measure assumes that one work has one identifier. With raw bibliographic data, the same reference is often written in several ways (spelling, abbreviations, missing years), each spelling becomes a different target_id, and two documents citing the same work in different ways no longer share it. This matters most for co-citation, where cited works are the nodes: a work split into several spellings is split into several nodes, each with a fraction of its citations. It matters less when the database gives an identifier to each cited reference (e.g. the identifiers of Scopus, OpenAlex or Web of Science), but even then references that the database could not match are missing or duplicated. Clean and match references before building networks, and check the most cited nodes for duplicates.

References

Domagalski R, Neal ZP, Sagan B (2021). “Backbone: An R Package for Extracting the Backbone of Bipartite Projections.” PLOS ONE, 16(1), e0244363. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0244363 .

Kessler MM (1963). “Bibliographic Coupling between Scientific Papers.” American Documentation, 14(1), 10–25. doi:10.1002/asi.5090140103 .

Neal Z (2014). “The Backbone of Bipartite Projections: Inferring Relationships from Co-Authorship, Co-Sponsorship, Co-Attendance and Other Co-Behaviors.” Social Networks, 39, 84–97. doi:10.1016/j.socnet.2014.06.001 .

Neal ZP (2022). “backbone: An R Package to Extract Network Backbones.” PLOS ONE, 17(5), e0269137. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0269137 .

Sen SK, Gan SK (1983). “A Mathematical Extension of the Idea of Bibliographic Coupling and Its Applications.” Annals of Library Science and Documentation, 30(2), 78–82.

Shen S, Zhu D, Rousseau R, Su X, Wang D (2019). “A Refined Method for Computing Bibliographic Coupling Strengths.” Journal of Informetrics, 13(2), 605–615. doi:10.1016/j.joi.2019.01.012 .

Small H (1973). “Co-Citation in the Scientific Literature: A New Measure of the Relationship between Two Documents.” Journal of the American Society for Information Science, 24(4), 265–269. doi:10.1002/asi.4630240406 .

Vladutz G, Cook J (1984). “Bibliographic Coupling and Subject Relatedness.” Proceedings of the American Society for Information Science, 21, 204–207.

Zhao D, Strotmann A (2008). “Author Bibliographic Coupling: Another Approach to Citation-Based Author Knowledge Network Analysis.” In Proceedings of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, volume 45(1), 1–10. https://asistdl.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/meet.2008.1450450292.

See also

build_network() for a single network; biblionetwork::biblio_coupling(), biblionetwork::coupling_strength(), biblionetwork::coupling_similarity(), backbone::backbone_from_projection(). The next steps of the pipeline are add_clusters() and merge_dynamic_clusters().

Examples

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")

# Bibliographic coupling networks of the articles explaining the 1970s
# stagflation, one per decade
networks <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 13,
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
names(networks)
#> [1] "1975-1987" "1988-2000" "2001-2013"
networks[[1]]

# Co-citation: cited documents linked when the same documents cite them,
# with windows on the year of the citing documents
citations <- merge(
  transform(Ref_stagflation[, c("source_id", "target_id")],
            source_id = as.character(source_id), target_id = as.character(target_id)),
  nodes[, c("source_id", "source_year")],
  by = "source_id"
)
cited <- Ref_stagflation[!duplicated(Ref_stagflation$target_id),
                         c("target_id", "target_author", "target_year")]
cocitation <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = transform(cited, target_id = as.character(target_id)),
  directed_edges = citations,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_on = "target",
  time_in = "edges",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 13,
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_angle",
  edges_threshold = 2,
  compute_size = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
cocitation[[1]]

# Authors linked by the references of the documents they sign
by_author <- merge(
  transform(Authors_stagflation, source_id = as.character(source_id)),
  citations, by = "source_id"
)
author_coupling <- build_network(
  nodes = data.frame(author_name = unique(by_author$author_name)),
  directed_edges = by_author,
  source_id = "author_name",
  target_id = "target_id",
  document_id = "source_id",
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_strength",
  edges_threshold = 2
)

# \donttest{
# Statistical backbone: keep the ties that random networks with the same
# degrees would rarely produce
if (requireNamespace("backbone", quietly = TRUE)) {
backbones <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 20,
  projection_method = "statistical",
  model = "sdsm",
  alpha = 0.05,
  backbone_args = list(mtc = "holm"),
  verbose = FALSE
)
}
